prime.problem: Ten cards of small steps are easy to finish as ten separate tricks. Without the causal map that joins them, you can retype micrograd but can't say why the loop needs zero_grad, or why += and the topological sort both exist.
prime.fits: This is the front page of course 2, read first as the map or last as the recap. It builds on the toolkit's slopes-multiply-along-a-chain idea, and every later course (bigram to GPT-2) runs the same four-step loop on tensors.
expect: backprop = local derivatives multiplied back from L.grad = 1
prime.goal: Draw the whole course as one causal map, from nudge ratio to training loop, and for each lever (h, step size, bias, = vs +=, lr, zero_grad) say what it changes and the number it produced.

attend: Which card first makes the gradient exact rather than estimated, and what did it replace?
The formula's ∂L/∂p is one symbol; which four cards does it take to compute it for all 41 parameters automatically?
Why does the same += appear twice in the causal map, once as a fix and once as the reason for a new step in the loop?
Which levers in the table change only precision or bookkeeping, and which change what the net learns?
What does the lecture never scale up that the next course has to, and which card hints at it?

must: A slope is a nudge ratio → estimating it per input costs one extra forward pass each and is approximate → record the forward pass as a graph of Values instead → the chain rule walked back from L.grad = 1 gives every gradient exactly in one pass

Each op knows only its local derivative (+ → 1, × → the other input, tanh → 1 − o²) → store it as a _backward closure → reverse topological order guarantees a node's grad is complete before it is passed on → one backward() call works for any graph

A node reached by several paths needs the sum of their gradients → closures use += onto grads that start at 0 → grads never reset themselves → the loop must zero_grad before every backward, or stale gradients act like a growing step size
The gradient points toward more loss → step every parameter by −lr × grad → forward, zero_grad, backward, update, repeated → loss 6.0054 → 0.0178 in 20 steps with lr 0.1 on MLP(3, [4, 4, 1])
elevated: One Python object per scalar → every step is visible and PyTorch still agrees to 6 decimals → but the per-node overhead makes it hopeless beyond toy nets → the same math moves to tensors next
reference: the chapter timestamps and the card-by-card numbers (L = −8, o = 0.7071)
the lever values in the table (h = 0.001, b = 6.8813735870195432, seed 1337)

compress.prompt: Course-level compress: without looking, draw the whole course's causal map on one page. Start from "a slope is a nudge ratio" and end at "loss falls". Put the ten cards as boxes in the order they are needed, draw an arrow for each because, and mark the two places where a missing piece gives a silent wrong answer.
checklist: nudge ratio → partials, one per input → too slow and approximate for many inputs
Value records the graph → chain rule walked backwards gives exact grads (plus copies, times swaps, tanh × 1 − o²)
a small step along the grads moves L as predicted, which is why grads are worth having
closures + reverse topological order automate the walk; += makes reused nodes correct
PyTorch computes the same grads, so the engine is right; the MLP + loss + loop turns it into training
silent failures: = instead of +=, and a missing zero_grad

retrieve.q: Explain to a programmer who has never trained a net why the whole lecture reduces to the single line p.data += -lr * p.grad, and what the other two hours are for.
answer: the line is gradient descent: step each parameter against the direction that increases the loss
everything before it exists to compute p.grad = ∂L/∂p for every parameter
exactly and in one backward pass: Value graph, chain rule, closures, topological order, +=
the MLP and loss only turn a question (fit these 4 targets) into one number L to differentiate

retrieve.q: Walk through one iteration of the training loop on MLP(3, [4, 4, 1]) and say, at each step, which card's machinery runs and what state changes.
answer: forward: the MLP's Neuron/Layer calls build a fresh graph of Values ending in L (value-object, a-neuron, mlp)
zero_grad: all 41 p.grad set to 0, clearing the last step's sums
backward: L.grad = 1, reverse topological order, each _backward adds local derivative × out.grad (automatic-backward, accumulate-gradients)
update: each p.data moves by −0.1 × p.grad; only parameters change, never the data xs

retrieve.q: Across the levers table, a wrong =, a missing zero_grad and a too-small h all give numbers without crashing. Rank them by how hard they are to notice, and say which check catches each.
answer: h too small: visibly wrong only if you compare with the exact rule (10.66 vs 14); keep h near 0.001
= instead of +=: forward values are all correct and the error depends on graph shape; a numerical gradient check or PyTorch comparison catches it
missing zero_grad: the hardest, because on an easy problem the loss can even end lower (0.000000); watch for jumps (3.78 at step 11) or compare with and without the reset
general lesson: check gradients against an independent source, not against "it trains"

retrieve.q: Why can you split tanh into exp, −, +, ÷ and get the same gradients, and what do you pay for doing so?
answer: the chain rule multiplies local derivatives along the path, and the product over the pieces equals tanh's own slope 1 − o² = 0.5
node e feeds two branches, so += is needed for the pieces to add up correctly
the cost is bookkeeping: 18 nodes instead of 10 to store and walk
a single op with a hand-written backward is shorter and faster, which is why PyTorch ships one

compare.q: The toolkit's first big idea says slopes multiply along a chain and add across paths. This course builds an engine around that one sentence. Which parts of micrograd implement the multiply half and which the add half, and what would break if either were missing?
answer: multiply: each _backward does local derivative × out.grad, applied in reverse topological order
add: += onto grads that start at 0, for nodes reached by several paths
without multiply there is no backprop at all; without add, reused nodes get one share (b = a + a gives 1, not 2)
the toolkit states the math on paper; micrograd makes it run for any graph without you choosing the order

compare.q: The big-ideas card states six claims; this overview gives one formula and a loop. Which claims does the formula p ← p − lr · ∂L/∂p already contain, and which ones only show up in the loop or the levers table?
answer: contained: a net is an expression ending in L (the loss), the derivative as sensitivity (∂L/∂p), backprop computes it
only in the loop: zero_grad, and why accumulated grads make it necessary
only in the levers and checks: that micrograd and PyTorch agree, that = vs += matters
the formula says what to compute; the cards say how to compute it without silent errors

predict.q: The next lecture trains on 228,146 character pairs with 27 × 27 = 729 weights. If you built each example's 27 logits as micrograd dot products (27 multiplies and 27 adds per logit), roughly how many Value objects would a single forward pass over the data create, and what does that tell you the next course must change?
predict.answer: 27 logits × (27 + 27) = 1,458 multiply/add nodes per example, before the softmax and loss. Times 228,146 examples = 332,636,868, about 3.3 × 10⁸ Python objects for one forward pass. That is why z2h-3 moves to tensors: one graph node per whole matrix operation, with the same gradients (this course's PyTorch check already showed the math doesn't change).

apply.task: Do Karpathy's exercise Colab using only your own engine from this course. Section 1: for f(a,b,c) = −a³ + sin(3b) − 1/c + b^2.5 − a^0.5 at (2, 3, 4), write the analytical gradient, then a one-sided and a symmetric numerical estimate. Section 2: add the ops you need (exp, log, division) so that softmax(logits) and -probs[3].log() backprop, and compare with torch.
apply.done: Section 1 prints [-12.353553390593273, 10.25699027111255, 0.0625] analytically and your symmetric estimate is closer to it than the one-sided one; section 2 gives grads [0.04177, 0.83902, 0.00565, -0.88645] for logits [0.0, 3.0, -2.0, 1.0], and torch agrees.
apply.hint: You need a log op with local derivative 1/x, and sin can be done in plain floats for section 1. If a grad is off by exactly one branch's share, look for an = that should be +=.
